Title: Cron Expression Parser
Description: Explain a cron expression in plain language, validate every field and list the next 5 run times in your local time zone. Presets and @macros included.
Keywords: cron expression parser, cron validator, explain cron expression, crontab syntax, next cron run, cron schedule checker

ParseToSeeResult: Enter a cron expression to see the description
ScheduleYearly: Once a year at midnight on January 1st
ScheduleMonthly: Once a month at midnight on the first day
ScheduleWeekly: Once a week at midnight on Sunday
ScheduleHourly: Every hour at the beginning of the hour

Seo_Introduction: Type a five-field cron expression or an @macro and see in plain words when it runs, what each field means and the next five run times. The check is strict, so a typo such as minute 61 or a step of */0 is pointed out instead of being ignored.
Seo_DetailedDescription:
Supported syntax: `*`, single values, ranges `1-5`, lists `1,15`, steps `*/15` and `0-30/10`, month names `JAN`–`DEC`, weekday names `SUN`–`SAT`, `7` as Sunday, `L` (last day of the month) and `?` in the day fields, plus `@yearly`, `@monthly`, `@weekly`, `@daily`, `@hourly` and `@reboot`. Every field is checked against its range, and the error names the field and the allowed values.

The description is written in your interface language — for example `0 9 * * MON-FRI` reads “At 09:00 Monday through Friday”. When both day of month and day of week are restricted, the tool follows the Vixie cron rule: the job runs when either of them matches. Next run times are calculated in your browser's time zone, up to 30 years ahead; a date that never occurs (`0 0 30 2 *`) is reported as having no upcoming runs.

Results update as you type, and quick preset buttons fill in common schedules. The next runs can be shown in several date formats — ISO 8601 with the time-zone offset, US style, your locale and others; the chosen format is remembered. Nothing is sent to a server.
Seo_Examples:
**Nightly backup**: `0 2 * * *` — “Every day at 02:00”.

**Polling**: `*/15 * * * *` — “Every 15 minutes”.

**Month-end report**: `0 0 L * *` — “At 00:00 on the last day of the month”.

**Day of month OR weekday**: `0 0 13 * 5` — “At 00:00 on the 13th of the month or on Fridays”: it runs on every 13th and on every Friday, not only on Friday the 13th.
Seo_HowToSteps:
### Step 1: Enter the expression
Type it into the **Cron Expression** field or click one of the **Quick Presets**.

### Step 2: Read the explanation
**Human Readable** shows the schedule in words, and **Expression Parts** lists what each of the five fields means.

### Step 3: Check the run times
Look at **Next Execution Times** and switch the **Date format** if needed.

### Step 4: Copy
Click **Copy** to copy the description, for example into a code comment.
Seo_Tips:
- Cron has no time-zone field: the server runs jobs in its own zone (often UTC), while the times here are in your browser's zone.
- Only the classic five fields are supported; Quartz-style expressions with seconds or a year field are rejected.
- A step restarts in every larger unit: `0 */7 * * *` runs at 00:00, 07:00, 14:00 and 21:00, then again at 00:00.
- `@reboot` runs once at system start, so it has no next run times.
- To build an expression from separate fields, use the Cron Expression Generator.
TimelineHorizon: Only {0} runs within the next {1} years — the search stops there.
TimelineHorizon_one: Only {0} run within the next {1} years — the search stops there.
TimelineReboot: @reboot runs once each time the cron daemon starts, so there are no future times to list.
TimelineRules: Times are local. When both day of month and weekday are restricted, a day matching either one runs (standard cron). A time skipped by a daylight-saving change moves forward; a repeated hour runs once.
